planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from the base in spring when repotting into fresh, chunky, well-drained mix; Atom is self-heading and needs no moss pole or climbing support.

directions: Atom is a compact, self-heading philodendron bred as a dwarf, tidier alternative to the sprawling tree philodendron (Selloum), with deeply cut, ruffled, dark green lobed leaves held on short, thick petioles in a dense rosette. It never develops a climbing habit or long internodes, so it stays neat and shrubby on a tabletop or floor without staking. Slow to moderate growth and tolerance of average indoor light make it forgiving for a first-time aroid grower, though leaf lobing is most pronounced with brighter indirect light. Let the top inch or two of chunky potting mix dry between waterings and wipe dust from the leaves periodically so they can photosynthesize efficiently.

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; pink coloring intensifies in brighter light but the plant still tolerates dim interiors.

directions: Lady Valentine forms an upright clump of broad, lance-shaped leaves marbled in shades of cream, green, and rose-pink, with pink-tinged petioles and stems that echo the leaf coloring. It belongs to the modern group of Thai-bred colored Aglaonema hybrids selected for bolder pigment than most species and older cultivars show. Foliage color holds up reasonably well in typical indoor light but becomes more vivid with bright, indirect exposure, while direct sun bleaches or scorches the leaves. Allow the top inch or two of potting mix to dry between waterings, keep it above 60°F away from cold drafts, and repot every couple of years as the clump fills its container.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; speckling shows best in bright, indirect light.

directions: Pink Dalmatian carries dense, irregular pink speckling scattered across a green background on each broad, pointed leaf, an appearance that gives the cultivar its spotted-coat namesake and distinguishes it from the more evenly marbled pink Aglaonema hybrids. Like other colored Aglaonema selections, it forms an upright clump from a short, suckering base and tolerates low to moderate indoor light, though the pink speckling is most vivid with bright, indirect exposure. It is a slow to moderate grower that prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings, since soggy, poorly drained mix quickly leads to root and stem rot. Keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and divide crowded clumps when repotting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

planting.note: Root stem cuttings with at least one node in moist potting mix or water in spring or summer; the cream leaf margins hold their color best in bright, indirect light.

directions: Variegated cupid peperomia trails or climbs on thin, wiry stems lined with heart-shaped, glossy leaves edged in an irregular band of creamy white, a variegated sport of the plain green species that is often mistaken at a glance for a small-leaved philodendron. It is easy to grow in a hanging basket or trained up a small support, with semi-succulent leaves and stems that store some water, making it more forgiving of missed waterings than thinner-leaved houseplants. Bright, indirect light keeps the cream variegation crisp; low light causes new growth to revert toward solid green. Let the potting mix dry noticeably between waterings and use a well-drained, chunky mix to avoid stem rot.

common_name: Red Spot Tricolor Syngonium (Speckled Arrowhead Plant)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings with a node in moist potting mix or water in spring or summer; speckled variegation shows best in bright, indirect light.

directions: Red Spot Tricolor carries arrow-shaped, deep green leaves flecked with irregular cream and soft pink speckling scattered across the blade rather than following the veins, giving it a stippled, painterly look distinct from the more evenly striped or blushed arrowhead cultivars. Young plants hold an upright, bushy form and can be trained onto a moss pole as they mature, where the leaves develop the deeper lobes typical of adult syngonium foliage. Pinch growing tips to keep the plant compact, provide bright indirect light for the strongest speckling, and let the top inch of potting mix dry between waterings. Sap can irritate skin and is toxic if ingested by pets or people.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Tricolor's pink new growth and cream margins color best with strong indirect light.

directions: Tricolor is one of the oldest and most recognizable variegated wax plant cultivars, with thick, waxy leaves edged in a creamy white margin that flushes deep pink to burgundy on new growth before settling toward cream as leaves mature, giving each vine three distinct colors at once. Like other Hoya carnosa forms, it is a twining vine best grown on a trellis or in a hanging basket, producing rounded clusters of small, fragrant, star-shaped pink flowers from the same reusable spurs year after year, so those spurs should never be pruned off. Bright indirect light produces the strongest pink blush and keeps growth compact; low light causes the plant to green out and stretch. Let the chunky, fast-draining mix dry between waterings.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; silver speckling shows best with strong indirect light.

directions: Splash is a heavily silver-speckled selection of Hoya pubicalyx, with narrow, semi-succulent, dark green leaves dusted in irregular flecks of silvery gray that give the vine a mottled, spattered look distinct from the more solid or evenly striped pubicalyx forms in cultivation. It is a vigorous, fast-growing twining vine best trained onto a trellis or hoop, eventually producing clusters of small, dark maroon to near-black star-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening. Bright, indirect light brings out the strongest silver speckling and encourages flowering, while low light produces plainer, greener foliage. Let the chunky, fast-draining mix dry between waterings and feed lightly during active growth.
